comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological claims (C73, C74, C75). Both evaluations support the dataset size, phylogenetic methods, and publication bias arguments without reservation.

Strong agreement on claims about differential effects across clutch size gradient (C21, C59, C60, C83). Both evaluations support that trade-offs emerge when species are pushed beyond natural limits, particularly for small-clutch species.

Agreement on variance partitioning and phylogenetic analysis claims (C23, C24, C25). Both evaluations support these statistical findings and accept the acknowledged limitations regarding phylogenetic inference.

Agreement on limitations and assumptions (C64, C65, C66, C67, C68). OpenEval explicitly supports these as appropriate caveats, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the focus on survival costs without challenging the assumptions.

Agreement on quality masking hypothesis (C42, C43, C61, C72). Both evaluations support this interpretation, with OpenEval citing quantitative evidence and peer reviewers endorsing it as an important contribution to understanding trade-offs.

Partial agreement on meta-analysis findings (C3, C4, C16, C17, C18). Both support opposite effects in experimental vs. observational studies. Peer R1 also covers quality masking claims (C5, C41, C54) that OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

Agreement on quality masking evidence (C5, C41, C54, C55, C56). OpenEval supports the counterbalancing interpretation with quantitative evidence, while peer reviewers affirm the study 'effectively separates the effects of individual quality from reproductive costs.'

Agreement on proportional scaling methodology (C20, C19, C81). OpenEval supports the methodological rationale, and peer reviewers implicitly accept it by not challenging the approach and describing evidence as 'solid.'
Agreement on lack of sex differences (C22). OpenEval supports this finding while noting unexplained contradiction with prior work; peer reviewers implicitly accept without raising concerns.

Significant disagreement on fitness projection claims (C7, C26, C27, C28, C29, C30, C32, C33, C62). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to untested assumptions about linearity, constant effect sizes, and ignored fitness costs. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the flat fitness landscape interpretation without challenge.

Major disagreement on overarching conclusions (C8, C9, C37, C38, C39, C40, C63, C70). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the conclusion extends beyond data and conflates statistical non-significance with biological irrelevance. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, explicitly endorsing that 'reproductive-survival trade-offs are minimal in birds.'

Disagreement on fitness projection sensitivity analyses (C28, C29, C30). OpenEval expresses uncertainty about assumptions underlying these projections, while peer reviewers accept them as supporting the minimal trade-off conclusion.

Partial agreement on weak experimental effects (C2). Both support that costs are small/inconsistent, but OpenEval notes the claim 'questions theory's general validity' is overstated since trade-offs do exist when masked by quality effects. Peer reviewers accept the framing more directly.

OpenEval rates evolutionary dynamics claims (C31, C34, C35, C36) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative extrapolations lacking direct empirical support. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; peer R9 touches on C36 but doesn't evaluate the evolutionary claims.
OpenEval supports literature contextualization claims (C45-C51) as appropriately cited and connected to findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval rates speculative alternative explanations (C52, C53, C57, C58) as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging they are plausible but untested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports foundational life-history theory claims (C1, C10-C15, C44) as appropriately cited background. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
